summary: An older edition of the periodic list of Internet protocol standards. It explained the standardization process and the RFC series, defined the terms used, and listed protocols at each stage of standardization. This edition is historic and was replaced by RFC 2400.

plainLanguage.summary: A big report card listing which internet rules were official, which were drafts, and which were just ideas. It has since been replaced by newer report cards.

questions: what are internet official protocol standards
subtitle: The Internet Architecture Board's periodic snapshot of which protocols are standards.

tldr.problem: As new Internet protocols are developed, the community needs to know which ones are official standards, which are still drafts, and which are experimental or obsolete.
tldr.mechanism: The Internet Architecture Board publishes a periodic list categorizing all protocols by their maturity level (Standard, Draft Standard, Proposed Standard, Experimental, Informational, or Historic) and requirement level (Required, Recommended, Elective, Limited Use, or Not Recommended).
tldr.outcome: This 1998 edition documented the state of standards at that time. It is now Historic and was replaced by RFC 2400 a few months later, which reflected more recent additions and changes.

today: RFC 2300 is Historic. It was superseded by RFC 2400 just four months later. The Internet Standards Board now publishes updated protocol standards lists periodically on their web pages, and the authoritative source is maintained at the RFC Editor's website rather than in a single RFC document.

sections.title: The Standardization Process
sections.content:
The Internet Architecture Board (IAB) maintains the authoritative list of which protocols have become Internet standards. The Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) develops these protocols in working groups, and the Internet Engineering Steering Group (IESG) makes the final standardization decisions.

Protocols follow a maturity ladder: new protocols start as Proposed Standards, can advance to Draft Standards after at least two implementations and six months of review, and finally become Standards when they demonstrate operational interoperability. The RFC explains that IETF advancement decisions require recommendation from the IESG, and there are minimum delays (6 months to draft, 4 months to standard) to allow community review.
sections.plainLanguage: Internet protocols go through levels like leveling up in a game: first Proposed (maybe it will work), then Draft (we are testing it), then Standard (it is official). The Internet Architecture Board keeps the official scoreboard.

sections.title: Protocol Categories and Requirement Levels
sections.content:
Every protocol in the list occupies a cell in a two-dimensional matrix. The first axis is maturity level (the protocol's state of standardization): Standard, Draft Standard, Proposed Standard, Experimental, Informational, or Historic. Historic protocols have been superseded or are otherwise unused.

The second axis is requirement level (what systems must do): Required (all systems must implement), Recommended (systems should implement), Elective (optional), Limited Use (only for specific circumstances), or Not Recommended (avoid). For example, a protocol might be a Standard-Elective (officially standardized but optional to implement), or Experimental-Limited Use (still being researched and only for specialized uses).
sections.plainLanguage: Each protocol gets two labels: its maturity (is it official, a draft, or an experiment?) and its requirement (do you have to use it, should you use it, or is it optional?)

sections.title: Understanding the Terms
sections.content:
A Standard Protocol is one the IESG has officially approved for Internet use; these receive STD numbers. Draft Standard protocols are under active consideration and need substantial testing. Proposed Standard protocols are candidates for standardization, and implementation by several groups is encouraged.

Experimental protocols should only be used by researchers coordinating with the protocol's developer; they are not intended for general use. Informational protocols come from other standards bodies or vendors and are published for the Internet community's convenience. Historic protocols are unlikely to become standards because they have been superseded or have lost community interest. Protocols not yet on the standards track at all—such as vendor protocols or early research work—do not appear in this list.
sections.plainLanguage: Standard means the Internet approved it. Draft means they are still testing it. Proposed means maybe it will be approved. Experimental means researchers are playing with it. Informational means it came from somewhere else. Historic means nobody uses it anymore.

sections.title: The Protocol Listings
sections.content:
The RFC contains sections listing protocols in each category. Section 6.1 describes recent changes (new RFCs and movements between categories). Sections 6.2 through 6.10 list the actual protocols, organized by maturity level: Standard Protocols, Draft Standard Protocols, Proposed Standard Protocols, Telnet Options, Experimental Protocols, Informational Protocols, Historic Protocols, and Obsolete Protocols.

For most protocols listed, the RFC documents related standards such as the Assigned Numbers registry (which lists protocol numbers, port numbers, and other constants), Gateway Requirements (for routers), and Host Requirements (for end systems). These companion documents provide detailed guidance and clarification beyond the basic protocol specifications.
sections.plainLanguage: The rest of the RFC is a big list: here are all the Standard protocols, here are the Drafts, here are the Experiments, and so on. Each one says whether you need to use it and what version of the RFC to read.

sections.title: Scope and Updating
sections.content:
This edition (RFC 2300, May 1998) explicitly supersedes twelve earlier editions in the same series (RFCs 2200, 2000, 1920, 1880, 1800, 1780, 1720, 1610, 1600, 1540, 1500, and 1410), going back to the first such document. The RFC is issued periodically, roughly every 100 RFCs, to keep the list current as new protocols are developed and old ones are retired.

The RFC notes that this edition is itself Historic and was almost immediately superseded by RFC 2400 (September 1998), which reflected additional new protocols and status changes in just the four months between publications. Readers are advised that they should always ensure they have the current edition, as it is the reference document for determining which RFC documents the current specification of each protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: This list gets updated a few times a year because new protocols are created and old ones change status. This particular copy is from May 1998, and a newer one came out a few months later.
